317: It is a matter of deep regret that we lack original evidence for the last remarkable days of our friend.
We are therefore obliged to break off the course of his correspondence, and to fill the gap with a connected narrative.
318: I have felt it my duty to collect accurate information from the mouths of people well acquainted with his history.
The story is simple, and all the accounts agree except in a few unimportant particulars.
It is true that where the characters of the people concerned are in question, opinions and judgments vary.
319: We have only, then, to relate conscientiously the facts our diligent labour has enabled us to collect, to give the letters of the deceased, and to pay close attention to the slightest fragment from his pen.
This is the more necessary because it is so difficult to discover the real and correct motives of men who are not of the common order.
320: Sorrow and discontent had taken deep root in Werther's soul, and gradually gave their character to his whole being.
The harmony of his mind was completely disturbed.

A perpetual excitement and mental irritation, which weakened his natural powers, had the saddest effects on him, and made him at length the victim of an exhaustion he struggled against with more painful effort than he had ever shown in contending with his other misfortunes.
His mental anxiety wore away his various good qualities, and he was soon turned into a gloomy companion, always unhappy, and more unjust in his ideas the more wretched he became.
This, at least, was the opinion of Albert's friends.
They assert, moreover, that Albert's own character had undergone no change in the meantime: he was still the same man Werther had loved, honoured, and respected from the beginning.
His love for Charlotte was unbounded; he was proud of her, and wished her to be recognised by everyone as the noblest of created beings.
Was he to blame, then, for wishing to keep every appearance of suspicion away from her?
Or for being unwilling to share his rich prize with another, even for a moment, and in the most innocent way?

It is said that Albert often withdrew from his wife's room during Werther's visits; but this came from no hatred or aversion toward his friend, only from a feeling that his own presence was oppressive to Werther.
321: Charlotte's father, who was confined to the house by illness, used to send his carriage for her so that she could make excursions in the neighbourhood.
One day the weather had been unusually severe, and the whole country was covered with snow.
322: Werther went for Charlotte the following morning, so that if Albert were away he might bring her home himself.
323: The beautiful weather made little impression on his troubled spirit.
A heavy weight lay on his soul; a deep melancholy had taken hold of him, and his mind knew no change except from one painful thought to another.
324: As he now never knew any inward peace, the condition of his fellow creatures was a perpetual source of trouble and distress to him.
He believed he had disturbed the happiness of Albert and his wife; and while he blamed himself severely for it, he began to feel a secret dislike of Albert.
325: His thoughts turned to this point from time to time.
"Yes," he would say to himself, with ill-concealed dissatisfaction, "yes, this is after all the whole extent of that confiding, dear, tender, sympathetic love, that calm and eternal fidelity!"
"What do I see but satiety and indifference?"
"Does not every trivial engagement attract him more than his charming and lovely wife?"
"Does he know how to value his happiness?"
"Can he prize her as she deserves?"
"He possesses her, it is true — I know that, as I know much else, and I have grown used to the thought that he will drive me mad, or perhaps murder me."
"Is his friendship toward me still unimpaired?"
"Does he not see my attachment to Charlotte as an infringement of his rights, and my attentions to her as a silent reproach to himself?"
"I know, and indeed I feel, that he dislikes me, that he wishes me gone, that my presence is hateful to him."
326: He would often stop on his way to visit Charlotte and stand still, as though in doubt, seeming to want to turn back — and would go on all the same.
And, occupied with such thoughts and soliloquies as we have described, he would reach the hunting-lodge at last with a sort of involuntary consent.
327: On one occasion he entered the house; and, asking for Charlotte, he noticed that the household was in unusual confusion.
The eldest boy told him that a dreadful misfortune had happened at Walheim — that a peasant had been murdered.
This made little impression on him at first.
Going into the room, he found Charlotte reasoning with her father, who, in spite of his infirmity, insisted on going to the scene of the crime to hold an inquiry.
The criminal was unknown; the victim had been found dead at his own door that morning.
Suspicions were aroused: the murdered man had been in the service of a widow, and the man who had held the place before him had been dismissed from her employment.
328: As soon as Werther heard this he exclaimed, in great excitement, "Is it possible!"
"I must go to the spot — I cannot delay a moment!"
Every incident came back vividly to him, and he had not the slightest doubt that the murderer was the man he had so often spoken to and felt such regard for.
His way took him past the well-known lime trees to the house where the body had been carried, and the sight of that fondly remembered spot moved him deeply.
The threshold where the neighbours' children had so often played together was stained with blood; love and attachment, the noblest feelings of human nature, had turned into violence and murder.
The huge trees stood leafless and covered with hoarfrost; the beautiful hedgerows around the old churchyard wall were withered; and the gravestones, half covered with snow, showed through the gaps.
329: As he came near the inn, in front of which the whole village had gathered, screams were suddenly heard.
A troop of armed peasants was seen coming, and everyone cried out that the criminal had been taken.
Werther looked, and was not long in doubt.
The prisoner was none other than the servant who had been so attached to the widow, and whom he had met prowling about with that suppressed anger and ill-concealed despair we described before.
330: "What have you done, unfortunate man?" said Werther, going up to the prisoner.
The man turned his eyes on him in silence, and then answered with perfect composure: "No one will marry her now, and she will marry no one."
The prisoner was taken into the inn, and Werther left the place.
Werther's mind was fearfully stirred by this shocking business.
But he stopped being oppressed by his usual melancholy, moroseness, and indifference to everything around him.
He felt a strong pity for the prisoner, and was seized with an indescribable anxiety to save him from the fate hanging over him.
He thought him so unfortunate, thought his crime so excusable, and thought his own condition so nearly the same, that he was convinced he could make everyone else see the matter as he saw it himself.

He now became eager to undertake the man's defence, and began composing an eloquent speech for the occasion; and on his way to the hunting-lodge he could not keep himself from saying aloud the statement he meant to make to the judge.
331: When he arrived he found Albert had got there before him, and the meeting disconcerted him a little; but he soon recovered himself and put his opinion very warmly to the judge.

The judge shook his head doubtfully; and although Werther argued his case with the utmost zeal, feeling, and determination on behalf of his client, the judge was, as we may easily suppose, not much moved by his appeal.
On the contrary, he interrupted him in the middle of his address, reasoned with him seriously, and even rebuked him for becoming the advocate of a murderer.
He showed that on such a precedent every law might be broken and the public security utterly destroyed.
He added that in a case like this he could do nothing himself without incurring the greatest responsibility; everything must take its usual course and follow the ordinary channel.
332: Werther, however, did not give up his enterprise, and even begged the judge to connive at the prisoner's escape.
But this proposal was flatly rejected.
Albert, who had taken some part in the discussion, sided with the judge.
At this Werther grew enraged and took his leave in great anger, the judge having more than once assured him that the prisoner could not be saved.
333: How deeply this assurance grieved him may be judged from a note found among his papers, which was doubtless written on this very occasion.
334: I see clearly that we cannot be saved!"
335: Werther was highly incensed at the remarks Albert had made to the judge in the matter of the prisoner.

He thought he could detect a little bitterness in them toward himself; and although, on reflection, his sound judgment could not escape the fact that their view of the matter was correct, he felt the greatest possible reluctance to admit it.
336: A memorandum of Werther's on this point, expressing his general feelings toward Albert, has been found among his papers.
337: "What is the use of my constantly repeating that he is a good and estimable man?
He is an inward torment to me, and I am incapable of being just to him."
338: One fine evening in winter, when the weather seemed inclined to thaw, Charlotte and Albert were walking home together.
She looked about her from time to time, as if she missed Werther's company.
Albert began to speak of him, and blamed him for his prejudices.
He alluded to his unfortunate attachment, and said he wished it were possible to break off the acquaintance.
"I want it for our own sake," he added. "And I ask you to make him change his manner toward you, and visit you less often."
"The world is censorious, and I know that we are talked about here and there."
Charlotte made no reply, and Albert seemed to feel her silence.
At least, from that time he never spoke of Werther again; and when she brought the subject up, he let the conversation die away, or turned it into another channel.
339: The vain attempt Werther had made to save the unhappy murderer was the last feeble flicker of a flame about to go out.

He sank almost immediately afterwards into gloom and inactivity, until he was brought to complete distraction by learning that he was to be summoned as a witness against the prisoner, who was asserting his complete innocence.
340: His mind was now oppressed by the memory of every misfortune in his past life.
The humiliation he had suffered at the ambassador's, and the troubles that followed, revived in his memory.

Stripped of energy, he was cut off from every pursuit and occupation that makes up the business of ordinary life; and he fell victim to his own susceptibility, and to his restless passion for the most amiable and beloved of women, whose peace he destroyed.
In this unvarying monotony his days were consumed, and his powers were exhausted without aim or design, until they brought him to a sorrowful end.
341: A few letters he left behind, which we set down here, are the best proof of his anxiety of mind and the depth of his passion, and of his doubts and struggles, and his weariness of life.
343: Dear Wilhelm, I am reduced to the condition of those unfortunate wretches who believe they are pursued by an evil spirit.
Sometimes I am oppressed — not by apprehension or fear, but by an inexpressible inward sensation which weighs on my heart and stops my breath.
Then I wander out at night, even in this tempestuous season, and take pleasure in looking at the dreadful scenes around me.
344: A rapid thaw had suddenly set in; I had been told that the river had risen, that the brooks had all overflowed their banks, and that the whole vale of Walheim was under water.
On the stroke of twelve I hurried out.

The foaming torrents rolled down from the mountains in the moonlight; fields and meadows, trees and hedges were all confounded together, and the entire valley had become a deep lake, churned up by the roaring wind.
And when the moon came out and tinged the black clouds with silver, and the furious torrent at my feet foamed and thundered with an awful grandeur, I was overcome by a mixture of terror and delight.
With my arms stretched out I looked down into the yawning abyss and cried, "Plunge!"
For a moment my senses left me, in the intense delight of ending my sorrows and my sufferings with one plunge into that gulf.
And then I felt as though I were rooted to the earth and incapable of seeking any end to my misery.
But my hour has not yet come: I feel that it has not.
O Wilhelm, how willingly I would give up my existence to ride the whirlwind, or to embrace the torrent!
And then might not rapture, perhaps, be the portion of this liberated soul?
345: I turned my sorrowful eyes toward a favourite spot, where I used to sit with Charlotte under a willow after a tiring walk.
Alas, it was under water, and I could hardly even find the meadow.
And the fields around the hunting-lodge, I thought.
Has our dear bower been destroyed by this pitiless storm?
And a beam of past happiness fell on me, as the mind of a prisoner is lit up by dreams of flocks and herds and the old joys of home.
But I am free from blame.
I have the courage to die!

Perhaps I have — and yet here I still sit, like a wretched pauper woman who gathers faggots and begs her bread from door to door, to prolong for a few days a miserable existence she is unwilling to give up.
347: What is the matter with me, dear Wilhelm?
Is not my love for her of the purest, holiest, most brotherly kind?
Has my soul ever been stained by a single sensual desire?
But I will make no protestations.
And now, you visions of the night, how truly those mortals understood you who ascribed your various contradictory effects to some invincible power!
Last night — I tremble to admit it — I held her in my arms, locked in a close embrace.
I pressed her to my breast and covered with countless kisses those dear lips, which murmured soft protestations of love in reply.
My sight was confused by the delicious intoxication of her eyes.
Heavens! Is it sinful to revel in such happiness again, to call back those rapturous moments with intense delight?
My senses are bewildered, my memory confused, my eyes bathed in tears — I am ill, and yet I am well — I want nothing — I have no desires — it would be better if I were gone.
348: In the circumstances described above, a determination to leave this world had now taken firm possession of Werther's soul.

Since Charlotte's return this thought had been the final object of all his hopes and wishes; but he had resolved that such a step should not be taken in haste, but with calmness and tranquillity, and after the fullest deliberation.
349: His troubles and inward struggles may be understood from the following fragment, found undated among his papers, which seems to have been the beginning of a letter to Wilhelm.
350: "Her presence, her fate, her sympathy for me still have the power to draw tears from my withered brain."
351: "One lifts the curtain and passes through to the other side — that is all!
And why all these doubts and delays?
Because we do not know what is behind it — because there is no coming back — and because our mind infers that all is darkness and confusion where we have nothing but uncertainty."
352: His appearance was at last quite altered by the effect of these melancholy thoughts; and his resolution was now finally and irrevocably taken.
The following ambiguous letter, which he addressed to his friend, may seem to offer some proof of it.
354: I am grateful to your love, Wilhelm, for having repeated your advice so seasonably.
Yes, you are right: it is undoubtedly better that I should go.

But I do not entirely approve your plan of returning at once to your neighbourhood; at least I should like to make a little excursion on the way, particularly as we may now expect a steady frost, and good roads with it.
I am much pleased with your intention of coming to fetch me; only put off your journey a fortnight, and wait for another letter from me.
One should gather nothing before it is ripe, and a fortnight sooner or later makes a great difference.
Beg my mother to pray for her son, and tell her I ask her pardon for all the unhappiness I have caused her.
It has always been my fate to give pain to those whose happiness I should have furthered.
May every blessing of Heaven attend you!
